output.title: The real limit of dual running
output.body:
Dual running looks simple until you treat it as a real workflow decision. For a small business owner, it means keeping the manual process alive while an AI-assisted path runs beside it. That only makes sense when you are choosing between more manual work, another hire, or a bounded automation test on one repeatable workflow.

The catch is overlap. While both paths are live, someone still has to check outputs, resolve differences, and decide which version is the source of truth. If the workflow touches money movement or other high-risk decisions, human approval stays mandatory. The spreadsheet does not get a say.

Bareni’s normal sequence is to identify one recurring workflow, check honestly whether AI fits, and, if it does, define pilot scope, measures, and a fixed-price MVP. That is method, not a promise of results. Parallel running is useful only as a short learning phase before you decide whether the old process can be retired.

A practical next step is to ask yourself one question: how much owner time goes into this workflow each week, and how many decision points genuinely need your judgment? If the answer is “many,” dual running will be expensive for long. If it is narrow, a short pilot may be enough to show whether the new path deserves to stay.
